1: The Reference tab of the Federal Modernization Workbook holds six core pages that nobody reads front to back.
You open them when you need an answer: which command does this, which framework applies, where the Risk Management Framework is covered, whether a source is still current.
Two newer pages sit beside them on the site only, the Learn Coverage Map and the Zero Trust Closure Coverage tracker.
This briefing walks through each of the six core pages, the question it answers, and why the workbook would be weaker without it.
Then it shows how the pages fit together, who should open which one first, and how each page tells you how far to trust it.
2: Each book answers one question in depth, in reading order.
But an engineer, an I S S O or an authorizing official usually arrives with a question that cuts across all twenty-one books.
The Reference tab exists for those questions, and they fall into three kinds.
Run it: which command does the job, and which chapter teaches it.
Prove it: which federal requirement a piece of work supports, and what evidence an assessor would read.
Trust it: whether the sources behind all of this are still current.
Every page on the tab answers one of those three.
3: Here are the six pages, with the job each one does.
One page helps you run the kits: the Command Reference.
Four help you prove compliance: the Federal Framework Crosswalk, the RMF Map, the M nineteen seventeen and fye-cam Crosswalk, and the Microsoft Practice Crosswalk.
And one keeps everything trustworthy: the Source Register.
The next six slides take them one at a time.
The tab also carries two site-only pages, the Learn Coverage Map and the Zero Trust Closure Coverage tracker, which this briefing doesn't cover.
4: The Command Reference lists every command in the example kits: 718 of them across seventeen kits.
That is 615 functions exported by PowerShell modules, 55 PowerShell scripts and 48 Python tools.
What makes it trustworthy is how it's made.
The page is generated from each command's own help text every time the site builds.
If the help changes, the page changes with it, so the two never drift apart, and a public command without a synopsis or an example fails the check.
Each row also links back to the chapters and training modules that teach the command, so an engineer can go from what does this do, to where do I learn it, in one click.
5: The Federal Framework Crosswalk scores every book against the frameworks a federal modernization program answers to.
That goes well beyond security controls: how IT investments are chosen and funded, how enterprise architecture is kept, how digital services are delivered, and how privacy and records are handled.
Each book gets a score from zero, not addressed, to three, evidence-backed, for each framework, and the scores come from reading the chapters, not from counting keywords.
Just as important, the page checks each framework's current status at its primary source.

It found that O M B M twenty-two eighteen was rescinded by M twenty-six oh-five, the Federal Data Strategy is being retired, and the Federal Enterprise Architecture Framework survives only as history, while Circular A-130 still requires an enterprise architecture.
Executive Order 14028 is in force as amended, and FITARA has a new memo, M twenty-six ten.
Without that check, the books would cite frameworks that no longer apply.
6: The RMF Map is for the people who sign off: the I S S O, the control assessor and the authorizing official.
Their question is where the Risk Management Framework is in the workbook, and what each step leaves behind.
The books answer it chapter by chapter; this page puts the answer in one place.
It walks all seven steps of nist special publication eight hundred thirty-seven Revision 2 and their 47 tasks.
For each task it gives where the workbook treats it, the evidence an assessor would read, and the kit that produces it.
The marks today: 24 covered, 14 partial, 9 partial by design, where the workbook gives a template and a prompt because the decision belongs to the agency, and none not covered.
It also corrects a common mistake: FISMA isn't a level.
FISMA Moderate is shorthand for a categorization and a baseline.
The page is in review, waiting for a reviewer who didn't write the marks.
7: O M B M nineteen seventeen is the federal policy for identity, credential and access management.
It tells agencies to run identity as one program, to manage devices and automated technologies as well as people, to use piv and derived piv, and to federate.
The fye-cam Architecture breaks the same ground into services.
This crosswalk maps both to the workbook's books, guides and kits.
It starts with nine identity areas, from workforce and non-person identity to federation, governance and public identity.
Then it checks M nineteen seventeen section by section and the fye-cam services one by one.
Across those forty-two rows, the marks are 15 strong, 20 partial, 5 gaps, and 2 deliberately out of scope, with the reason stated.
Every mark comes from reading the linked pages.
Identity is where most of this program's work lands, so naming the gaps plainly matters as much as showing the strengths.
8: The books recommend Microsoft practices chapter by chapter: block legacy authentication, require phishing-resistant M F A, put privileged roles behind Privileged Identity Management, use device compliance as the access signal, connect servers through Azure Arc, and move sequel Server to Entra authentication.
This crosswalk puts 33 of those practices in one table.

Each row gives the practice and its chapter, the Microsoft Learn page that defines it, the automated check that confirms it, either a sis-uh ScubaGear policy I D or an Azure Policy built-in, and the date the row was last reviewed.
Seeing them side by side surfaced things no single chapter shows.
One policy carries two version numbers between ScubaGear and the B O D twenty-five oh-one list.
And Arc-enabled sequel Server has no built-in policy for Entra authentication, so it needs a custom check.
9: The Source Register is the foundation under everything else.
A slide or a video description doesn't link straight to a publisher's page.
It links to the source's row in this register, and the row links to the original.
That matters because a released deck or video can't change, but publishers move pages all the time.
With the register in between, a link in a released deck stays right: only the row has to change.
The register holds 540 sources today, under three rules.
A source's address is permanent: a row can be retired, but never deleted or renamed.
Every change goes through a reviewed pull request, adds to the revision history, and sends the page back to its owner for approval.
And the weekly source watch reads every row, shows the result in the Last scan column, and proposes fixes, but never edits on its own.
10: The pages aren't six separate lists; they build on each other.
The Federal Framework Crosswalk is the wide view, every book against every framework.
The RMF Map takes its Risk Management Framework row and goes task by task; where the two disagree, the map wins, and the crosswalk's RMF score is derived from it.
The M nineteen seventeen and fye-cam Crosswalk does the same deep dive for identity policy.
The Microsoft Practice Crosswalk shows the specific practices behind the evidence, each tied to an automated check, and the Command Reference lists the kit commands that produce that evidence.
Underneath all of them sits the Source Register, so every source the slides and videos cite has a permanent address that is checked every week.
11: So who should open which page first?
An engineer running the kits opens the Command Reference.
An I S S O or a control assessor opens the RMF Map.
An authorizing official reads the RMF Map, then the M nineteen seventeen and fye-cam Crosswalk.
A C I O or program lead starts with the Federal Framework Crosswalk.
An identity or cloud architect opens the Microsoft Practice Crosswalk.
And anyone citing a source uses the Source Register.
12: Finally, a reference page is only useful if you know how far to trust it, so each one tells you.
The marks come from reading the chapters, not counting keywords: every hit is opened in context, and false matches are dropped.
Each page shows its status, draft, in review or approved, and the date someone last reviewed it.
A page left unreviewed for more than 90 days is flagged on the page and in the weekly source-watch issue until someone reviews it.
And the gaps stay on the page.
Partial rows, gaps and out-of-scope items are listed with their reasons, and where no automated check exists, the row says so rather than inventing one.
Each of the six core pages also downloads as a Word document, and the Reference Set puts all six in one file, from the Reference tab or the Downloads page.
